summary.text: Bird flight is the main way most birds get around, and it also helps them feed, breed, escape predators and migrate.
Air flowing over a wing, which is an airfoil, produces lift; birds flap to turn that lift forward into thrust, since they have no engines.
Birds mainly use three types of flight, told apart by wing motion, and different species developed wing specializations for their environments, prey and predators.

facts.label: Forces at work
facts.value: Lift, drag and thrust, as on aircraft

facts.label: Hummingbird wingbeat
facts.value: About 43 beats a second; some others reach 80

facts.label: Hovering specialists
facts.value: Hummingbirds, the one family specialized for hovering

facts.value: Three limb bones: humerus, ulna and radius

facts.value: Take-off, one of the most energy-hungry parts of flight

items.prompt: A bird circles high with its wings held still and does not lose height. Where does the energy to stay up come from?

options.label: Its own height, spent bit by bit as it slowly sinks
Tiny wingtip flaps too quick for the eye to see
Warm rising air makes up for what drag takes away
Energy stored in its wing muscles, released slowly

items.explain: In gliding flight no propulsion is used; the energy lost to drag is either taken from potential energy or replaced by rising air currents called thermals.

items.prompt: A swan paddles across a lake in a long run before lifting off, yet a small bird simply jumps into the air. Why the difference?

options.label: Big birds need a running start to get enough airflow over the wing
Swans' wings only make lift while the bird touches water
Small birds' wings make thrust without any flapping
Swans must warm up their muscles before they can fly

items.explain: Take-off needs enough airflow across the wing to create lift. Small birds get it with a simple jump, but larger birds such as swans need a running start.

items.prompt: Hummingbirds hover; few big birds can for more than a moment. What explains that?

options.label: Large wings are too heavy to flap quickly
Hovering needs wings folded in, which big wings cannot do
Large bird bones are too thick to take the strain
True hovering makes lift by flapping alone, which takes a great deal of energy

items.explain: True hovering generates lift through flapping alone, which takes considerable energy and usually confines it to smaller birds.

items.prompt: Small birds on long trips often flap in bursts, then fold their wings against the body for a stretch. What is the likely benefit?

options.label: Less drag during the coasting stretch, and more efficient use of muscle
The folded body makes extra thrust on its own
The bird can hover in place between bursts
Warm rising air lifts the body while the wings rest

items.explain: Flap-bounding flight is believed to reduce the energy needed by cutting aerodynamic drag while the wings are folded, and to make muscle use more efficient.

items.prompt: A big bird must stop almost dead at its nest on a cliff ledge. Which approach works?

options.label: Fly straight at the ledge with wings folded to shed drag
Circle above the ledge and drop straight down onto it
Skid in using its feet as brakes, as it would on water
Aim below the nest, then pull up so its speed is nearly nil on arrival

items.explain: Some large birds aim for a point below the landing area, then pull up beforehand; if timed correctly the airspeed once the target is reached is virtually nil.

items.prompt: A hummingbird holds in place at a flower. What does its wing do differently from most other birds' during the stroke?

options.label: It folds inward on both strokes to cut drag
It stays extended in a figure-eight and lifts on both up- and down-stroke
It beats only on the down-stroke and rests on the up
It stays still while the body vibrates to make lift

items.explain: Most birds slightly fold the wing on the up-stroke, but the hummingbird wing is extended throughout a symmetrical figure-eight stroke and produces lift on both.

paragraphs.heading: What bird flight is
paragraphs.text: Flying is the main way most birds get around. It helps them find food, breed, escape predators and migrate. Flight covers several kinds of motion, from hovering to taking off and landing, each built from many complex movements. Over millions of years, species evolved specialized wings and styles of flight to suit their own environments, prey and predators.

paragraphs.heading: Lift, drag and thrust
paragraphs.text: Birds fly on principles similar to those of aircraft, held up by three aerodynamic forces: lift, drag and thrust. Lift comes from air flowing over the wing, which is an airfoil, a shape that makes the air push the wing up while the air itself is sent downward. Drag is the force that acts against the direction of travel, so it is where flight loses energy, and a streamlined body and wings reduce it. Aircraft get thrust from engines, but birds make it by flapping their wings with a certain amplitude and frequency.

paragraphs.heading: Gliding and flapping
paragraphs.text: Birds use three main kinds of flight, told apart by how the wings move. In gliding, no power is used and the upward force equals the bird's weight. The energy lost to drag is paid for either by losing height or by riding rising air currents called thermals, which is known as soaring. In flapping flight the wings still make lift, but the flight muscles tilt it forward to give thrust. The downstroke gives most of the thrust, and on each upstroke the wing folds in a little to save energy.

paragraphs.heading: Bounding and hovering
paragraphs.text: Small birds often cover long distances by bounding flight, in which short bursts of flapping alternate with spells when the wings are folded against the body and the bird follows a mostly ballistic path. This is thought to save energy by cutting drag during the folded phase. True hovering means making lift by flapping alone rather than by moving through the air, and its high energy cost usually limits it to smaller birds. Hummingbirds are the family specialized for it: their wings stay extended through a figure-of-eight stroke that makes lift on both the upstroke and the downstroke, beating some 43 times a second, and in others as many as 80.

paragraphs.heading: Taking off and landing
paragraphs.text: Taking off is one of the most energy-hungry parts of flight, because the bird must get enough air moving over its wings to make lift. Small birds simply jump upward. Larger birds such as albatrosses and swans need a running start, and large birds also face into the wind or drop off a branch or cliff. Landing is hard for large birds with high wing loads too; some aim below the target, such as a cliff nest, then pull up so they arrive with almost no airspeed. Some large birds such as geese lose height fast by sideslipping from side to side or even turning briefly upside down, a move called whiffling.

paragraphs.heading: Wings and their origins
paragraphs.text: The wings, which are a bird's forelimbs, are the key to flight. Each has a central vane built from three limb bones: the humerus, ulna and radius. Several theories try to explain how bird flight first evolved. They include falling or gliding down from trees, running or leaping up from the ground, running up slopes with help from the wings, and pouncing.
